text: Everything so far in this chapter has been S3 — object storage. EBS is a different animal entirely: network-attached block storage that gives an EC2 instance something closer to a virtual hard drive. This lesson covers what that means and the real rule governing how a volume attaches to an instance.

aws ec2 create-volume provisions a new EBS volume in a specific Availability Zone, not just a Region — that AZ choice matters, because it determines which instances the volume can ever attach to. Here, a 100 GB gp3 volume is created in us-east-1a.

S3 stores whole objects addressed by a key, accessed over HTTP. EBS is block storage — the same category as a physical disk, something the operating system formats, partitions, and mounts directly, the same way it would a drive bolted into the machine. The twist is that it's network-attached rather than physically inside the instance's host, so the data survives independently of the instance unless Delete on Termination is turned on, which many root volumes default to.

attach-volume connects an existing volume to a running instance at a device path like /dev/sdf. The one real constraint: the volume has to already sit in the same Availability Zone as the instance, because EBS doesn't span AZs. Moving a volume across AZs means snapshotting it first.

Two volume types cover almost every real workload. gp3 delivers a flat baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s regardless of size, and is the default choice for general-purpose workloads. io2 is built for demanding, low-latency needs like a busy transactional database, with a 99.999% durability guarantee higher than gp3's.

A volume, one instance, one Availability Zone, typically — that's the attachment model to remember, whether you're clicking through the console or scripting it with the CLI. Next up: EBS snapshots, the point-in-time, incremental backups that let you restore a volume, move it across AZs, or recover from a failure entirely.
